claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of single endogenous mitotic chromosomes from stage 3 and stage 8 embryo extracts (Figure 2A and B).

claims.claim: Chromosome widths increased by approximately 1.2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8.
claims.source: We found that median chromosome lengths decreased approximately 2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8 (Figure 2A and B), while chromosome widths increased only by ~1.2-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome widths from stage 3 and stage 8 embryo extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Shortening of the long axis is the predominant metric underlying the change in mitotic chromosome size during early embryogenesis.
claims.source: These changes were consistent with the magnitude of metaphase plate scaling during this period estimated by whole-embryo immunofluorescence (approximately 2-3-fold, Figure 1D) and demonstrates that shortening of the long axis is the predominant metric underlying the change in mitotic chromosome size during early embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the 2-fold decrease in chromosome length to the 1.2-fold increase in width, and consistency with metaphase plate volume changes.

claims.claim: The median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts.
claims.source: We also observed that the median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 2B), suggesting that replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements comparing endogenous stage 3 chromosomes to replicated sperm chromosomes in egg extracts (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
claims.source: We also observed that the median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 2B), suggesting that replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stage 3 chromosomes and replicated sperm chromosomes have similar lengths.

claims.claim: Combining metaphase-arrested egg extracts with stage 8 mitotic embryo extracts did not increase chromosome length.
claims.source: However, we observed no increase in chromosome length, indicating that mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mixing egg and stage 8 extracts 1:1 did not change embryo chromosome length (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
claims.source: However, we observed no increase in chromosome length, indicating that mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mixing egg and stage 8 extracts did not change chromosome length.

claims.claim: Sperm chromosomes formed in stage 8 extracts were at least 2-fold longer than endogenous stage 8 chromosomes.
claims.source: In both cases, sperm chromosomes were at least 2-fold longer than the endogenous stage 8 chromosomes (Figure 2D), suggesting that stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome lengths when sperm nuclei (replicated or unreplicated) were added to filtered stage 8 extracts (Figure 2D).

claims.claim: Stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
claims.source: In both cases, sperm chromosomes were at least 2-fold longer than the endogenous stage 8 chromosomes (Figure 2D), suggesting that stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sperm chromosomes formed in stage 8 extracts are longer than endogenous stage 8 chromosomes.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase.
claims.source: Thus, mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase, making mitotic chromosome scaling fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing that chromosome size cannot be changed by cytoplasmic factors during metaphase but can be changed by factors present during interphase.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling is fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
claims.source: Thus, mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase, making mitotic chromosome scaling fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the mechanisms of mitotic chromosome scaling to those of nuclear and spindle scaling.

claims.claim: G2-arrested nuclei isolated from blastula-stage embryos and added to metaphase egg extracts produced mitotic chromosomes approximately 2-fold shorter than replicated sperm chromosomes formed in the same extract.
claims.source: We next confirmed previous results that G2-arrested nuclei isolated from blastula-stage embryos and added to metaphase egg extracts produced mitotic chromosomes approximately 2-fold shorter than replicated sperm chromosomes formed in the same extract (Figure 3A and B; Kieserman and Heald, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths from stage 8 embryo nuclei and replicated sperm nuclei in egg extracts (Figure 3B), and is consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome size is determined prior to entry into metaphase, likely by chromatin factors loaded during interphase.
claims.source: This finding further supports the idea that mitotic chromosome size is determined prior to entry into metaphase, likely by chromatin factors loaded during interphase.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G2-arrested embryo nuclei produce short chromosomes when added to egg extracts.

claims.claim: A difference in chromosome size was recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation.
claims.source: A difference in chromosome size was also recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation, which are incapable of forming spindles but competent for mitotic chromosome assembly, indicating that spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that embryo chromosomes are shorter than sperm chromosomes in clarified extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling.
claims.source: A difference in chromosome size was also recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation, which are incapable of forming spindles but competent for mitotic chromosome assembly, indicating that spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome size differences persist in clarified extracts that cannot form spindles.

claims.claim: The magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished in clarified extracts (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts).
claims.source: However, the magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts), suggesting that the spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparing chromosome size differences in crude versus clarified extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: The spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
claims.source: However, the magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts), suggesting that the spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the magnitude of chromosome size difference is reduced in clarified extracts lacking membranes and spindles.

claims.claim: Embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei.
claims.source: We observed that embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the doubling of genome size due to the presence of both paternal and maternal genomes in embryo nuclei, suggesting that intranuclear DNA density is comparable between the two sources of nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear diameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claims.claim: Intranuclear DNA density is comparable between embryo nuclei and sperm nuclei.
claims.source: We observed that embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the doubling of genome size due to the presence of both paternal and maternal genomes in embryo nuclei, suggesting that intranuclear DNA density is comparable between the two sources of nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that embryo nuclei are 2-fold larger and contain twice the DNA (diploid vs. haploid).

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei.
claims.source: Yet, mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei (Figure 3B), while mitotic spindles formed with either source of nuclei were barely distinguishable in size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome lengths from embryo and sperm nuclei in egg extracts (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: Mitotic spindles formed with embryo nuclei or sperm nuclei were barely distinguishable in size.
claims.source: Yet, mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei (Figure 3B), while mitotic spindles formed with either source of nuclei were barely distinguishable in size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of spindle lengths formed with embryo or sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claims.claim: Neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size.
claims.source: These data suggest that neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size and further supports the idea that scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observations that embryo and sperm nuclei have different chromosome sizes despite similar DNA density and spindle sizes.

claims.claim: Scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
claims.source: These data suggest that neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size and further supports the idea that scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observations that these structures can scale independently of each other.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling could be recapitulated by adding embryo nuclei to metaphase-arrested egg extracts, but chromosome morphologies were distinct.
claims.source: Interestingly, although mitotic chromosome scaling could be recapitulated by adding embryo nuclei to metaphase-arrested egg extracts, chromosome morphologies were distinct.
claims.evidence: This is supported by observations comparing chromosome morphologies in embryo extracts versus egg extracts (Figure 2A vs. Figure 3C).

claims.claim: The separation of sister chromatid arms resulting in X-shaped mitotic chromosomes in embryo extracts was not observed when stage 8 embryo nuclei were added to egg extracts.
claims.source: The separation of sister chromatid arms resulting in X-shaped mitotic chromosomes in both stage 3 and stage 8 mitotic embryo extracts (Figure 2A) was not observed when stage 8 embryo nuclei were added to egg extracts as chromosome arms remained tightly associated along their lengths (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by visual comparison of chromosome morphologies in different extract conditions (Figure 2A vs. Figure 3C).

claims.claim: The factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts, while other factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome size is maintained but morphology changes when embryo nuclei are added to egg extracts.

claims.claim: Factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei when introduced into metaphase egg extracts.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts, while other factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome morphology changes when embryo nuclei are added to egg extracts.

claims.claim: Short embryo chromosomes contained less condensin I and topo II, but more histone H1.8 relative to long replicated sperm chromosomes.
claims.source: We found that short embryo chromosomes contained less condensin I and topo II, but more histone H1.8 relative to long replicated sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements of these proteins on embryo and sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: Condensin II is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract.
claims.source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claims.claim: Condensin II plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size.
claims.source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claims.claim: Lower levels of condensin II were observed on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes.
claims.source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claims.claim: Depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: These results are consistent with a study showing that depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes (Maresca et al., 2005) and more recent work showing that histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes (Choppakatla et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claims.claim: Histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: These results are consistent with a study showing that depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes (Maresca et al., 2005) and more recent work showing that histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes (Choppakatla et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claims.claim: Differential recruitment of condensins, topo II, or histone H1.8 may contribute to mitotic chromosome scaling during embryogenesis.
claims.source: Therefore, differential recruitment of condensins, topo II, or histone H1.8 may contribute to mitotic chromosome scaling during embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins are differentially abundant on short versus long chromosomes, and is consistent with published work on their functions.

claims.claim: Short embryo chromosomes can be reset to lengths observed in replicated sperm samples by cycling the mitotic chromosomes through an additional interphase in egg extracts.
claims.source: Our previous work showed that short embryo chromosomes could be reset to lengths observed in replicated sperm samples by cycling the mitotic chromosomes through an additional interphase in egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B; Kieserman and Heald, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing chromosome length changes after cycling through interphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), and is consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: The abundance of condensin I, topo II, and histone H1.8 increased in the second metaphase compared to the first metaphase for embryo chromosomes.
claims.source: To test whether the abundance of candidate scaling factors was affected, we performed immunofluorescence on mitotic embryo chromosomes formed during the first or second metaphase and found that the abundance of all three factors increased in the second metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements comparing first and second metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C-F).

claims.claim: Condensin I levels increased 2-fold in the second metaphase, returning to levels found on replicated sperm chromosomes.
claims.source: Of the three factors, condensin I levels increased the most (2-fold), returning to levels found on replicated sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D).

claims.claim: Condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8.
claims.source: Our observation that histone H1.8 levels increased slightly after the second metaphase suggests that condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8, and that condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that condensin I increased more than H1.8 in the second metaphase, and chromosomes lengthened.

claims.claim: Condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
claims.source: Our observation that histone H1.8 levels increased slightly after the second metaphase suggests that condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8, and that condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosomes lengthen in the second metaphase despite increased H1.8.

claims.claim: Short embryo chromosomes had increased longer-range genomic contacts along their entire length, as evidenced by thickening of the diagonal in Hi-C contact maps.
claims.source: Hi-C contact maps indicated that short embryo chromosomes had increased longer-range genomic contacts along their entire length, as evidenced by thickening of the diagonal (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data showing differences in contact maps between sperm and embryo chromosomes (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: The shape of P(s) for Xenopus mitotic chromosomes was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus, and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes.
claims.source: The shape of P(s) was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Gibcus et al., 2018; Naumova et al., 2013), and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes (Nand et al., 2021), indicating the same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes across diverse species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of P(s) curves to published data from other species.

claims.claim: The same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes exists across diverse species.
claims.source: The shape of P(s) was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Gibcus et al., 2018; Naumova et al., 2013), and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes (Nand et al., 2021), indicating the same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes across diverse species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of P(s) curves across species.

claims.claim: The amount of DNA contained within a layer is estimated by the genomic distance at which the derivative of P(s) is at its minimum, which was 10^6 bp for sperm chromosomes compared to ~10^7 bp for embryo chromosomes.
claims.source: Based on this previous work, the amount of DNA contained within a layer is estimated by the genomic distance at which the derivative is at its minimum, which was 106 bp for sperm chromosomes compared to ~107 bp for embryo chromosomes (Figure 4C, gray bar).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the derivative of P(s) from Hi-C data (Figure 4C), interpreted using previous models.

claims.claim: DNA loop size can be estimated from where the derivative of P(s) peaks at smaller genomic distances, which was between 10^4–10^5 bp for sperm chromosomes vs. 10^5–10^6 bp for embryo chromosomes.
claims.source: Within a layer, DNA loop size can be estimated from where the derivative peaks at smaller genomic distances, which was between 104–105 bp for sperm chromosomes vs. 105–106 bp for embryo chromosomes (Figure 4C, orange bar).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the derivative of P(s) from Hi-C data (Figure 4C), interpreted using previous models.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosomes scale smaller during development through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in larger DNA loops and more DNA per layer.
claims.source: Combined with our immunofluorescence results from Figure 3, these data are consistent with a model in which mitotic chromosomes scale smaller during development through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in larger DNA loops and more DNA per layer, thus accommodating more DNA on a shorter chromosome axis (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from combining immunofluorescence data showing lower condensin I on embryo chromosomes with Hi-C data showing larger loops and more DNA per layer.

claims.claim: Mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length approximately 1.3-fold.
claims.source: We found that mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length ~1.3-fold (Figure 5B), consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at the stage of development corresponding to the N/C ratios tested (stages 6–7, Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: The decrease in chromosome length due to increased N/C ratio was consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at stages 6-7.
claims.source: We found that mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length ~1.3-fold (Figure 5B), consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at the stage of development corresponding to the N/C ratios tested (stages 6–7, Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparing in vitro results to in vivo measurements.

claims.claim: The chromosome size change due to increased N/C ratio was accompanied by an approximately 1.6-fold decrease in condensin I abundance on mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: This size change was accompanied by an ~1.6-fold decrease in condensin I abundance on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 5C), with less significant changes for histone H1.8 and topo II (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: The increased N/C ratio did not significantly affect nuclear size.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear size at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: The increased N/C ratio increased spindle size.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements of spindle size at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5E).

claims.claim: The N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not nuclear or spindle size.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N/C ratio affects chromosome size but not nuclear size, and increases rather than decreases spindle size.

claims.claim: Both nuclei and spindles scale to compartment volume through a limiting-component mechanism.
claims.source: Previous work using lipid droplets to encapsulate spindles and nuclei in different sized compartments showed that both structures scale to compartment volume through a limiting-component mechanism (Chen et al., 2019; Good et al., 2013; Leech et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claims.claim: Maternal components do not become size-limiting for spindles and nuclei until later developmental stages.
claims.source: However, the range of N/C ratios (defined again as genome copies per volume cytoplasm) tested here was significantly lower (approximately 10-fold) than in those studies, suggesting that maternal components do not become size-limiting for spindles and nuclei until later developmental stages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the N/C ratios tested in this study to those in previous studies, and observing that spindles and nuclei did not scale as expected.

claims.claim: The major molecular determinants of mitotic chromosome size are loaded during interphase.
claims.source: Our previous data strongly suggested that the major molecular determinants of mitotic chromosome size are loaded during interphase.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing that chromosome size is set during interphase and cannot be changed during metaphase.

claims.claim: Varying the concentration of stage 8 embryo nuclei added to metaphase egg extracts had no effect on mitotic chromosome length.
claims.source: We tested this model further by varying the concentration of stage 8 embryo nuclei added to metaphase egg extracts and observed no difference in mitotic chromosome length (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).

claims.claim: Titration of maternal factors had already occurred in the embryo by the time nuclei were collected at G2.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with the idea that titration of maternal factors had already occurred in the embryo by the time nuclei were collected at G2.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that varying embryo nuclei concentration did not affect chromosome size.

claims.claim: When sperm chromosomes were added directly to metaphase egg extracts, there was no effect of N/C ratio on chromosome length.
claims.source: Also, when sperm chromosomes were added directly to metaphase egg extracts, thus skipping the initial round of replication, there was again no effect of N/C ratio on chromosome length (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claims.claim: The factors that set mitotic chromosome length as a function of N/C ratio are loaded during interphase, not metaphase.
claims.source: Thus, the factors that set mitotic chromosome length as a function of N/C ratio are loaded during interphase, not metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that N/C ratio only affects chromosome size when nuclei go through interphase in the extract.

claims.claim: Protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions.
claims.source: As predicted, although protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), the levels of all factors found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).

claims.claim: The levels of condensin I, H3, and histone H1.8 found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased.
claims.source: As predicted, although protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), the levels of all factors found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements of nuclei from different developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).

claims.claim: Maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable.
claims.source: Together these observations confirm that maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable and demonstrate that a higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protein levels per nucleus decrease as genome copy number increases, and that increasing N/C ratio in vitro decreases chromosome size and condensin I levels.

claims.claim: A higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
claims.source: Together these observations confirm that maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable and demonstrate that a higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that increasing N/C ratio decreases chromosome size and condensin I levels.

claims.claim: Importin α was previously identified as a factor that coordinately scales nuclei and spindles to cell size.
claims.source: We previously identified importin α as a factor that coordinately scales nuclei and spindles to cell size by regulating nuclear import of lamin proteins and the activity of a microtubule destabilizing protein, respectively (Brownlee and Heald, 2019; Levy and Heald, 2010; Wilbur and Heald, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Palmitoylation of importin α drives a fraction of the total protein to the cell membrane.
claims.source: Palmitoylation of importin α drives a fraction of the total protein to the cell membrane, where it can no longer bind to and inhibit its nuclear localization sequence (NLS)-containing cargo that regulates spindle size (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claims.claim: As cell size decreases during early cleavage divisions, cell surface area/volume (SA/V) increases, causing a larger fraction of importin α to associate with the plasma membrane.
claims.source: As cell size decreases during early cleavage divisions, cell surface area/volume (SA/V) increases, causing a larger fraction of importin α to associate with the plasma membrane, thus releasing more scaling factors into the cytoplasm (Figure 6A; Brownlee and Heald, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claims.claim: Mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment.
claims.source: We found that mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment and was fully rescued by the addition of purified recombinant importin α that cannot be palmitoylatated (NP importin α), but not by addition of wild-type (WT) importin α (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths in DMSO, palmostatin, and palmostatin + importin α conditions (Figure 6C).

claims.claim: The decrease in chromosome size due to palmostatin treatment was fully rescued by the addition of non-palmitoylatable importin α, but not by wild-type importin α.
claims.source: We found that mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment and was fully rescued by the addition of purified recombinant importin α that cannot be palmitoylatated (NP importin α), but not by addition of wild-type (WT) importin α (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 6C).

claims.claim: Palmostatin-treated chromosomes showed increased abundance of histone H1.8, whereas the levels of condensin I and topo II were unchanged.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence of DMSO- or palmostatin-treated chromosomes revealed increased abundance of histone H1.8 on short palmostatin-chromosomes, whereas the levels of condensin I and topo II were unchanged (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: Importin α partitioning scales mitotic chromosomes to cell size by increasing availability of histone H1.8 in the cytoplasm as cell SA/V increases.
claims.source: These data are consistent with our observation that short embryo chromosomes contain more histone H1.8 than long sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D) and suggest a model in which importin α partitioning scales mitotic chromosomes to cell size by increasing availability of histone H1.8 in the cytoplasm as cell SA/V increases.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that palmostatin treatment (mimicking higher SA/V) increases H1.8 on chromosomes and decreases chromosome size.

claims.claim: Palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes, while palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths when palmostatin was added during interphase versus metaphase (Figure 6F).

claims.claim: Palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes, while palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length (Figure 6F).

results.result: Mitotic chromosomes, spindles, and nuclei all scale continuously with cell size in vivo during Xenopus embryogenesis, but with different magnitudes. Nuclei decrease ~10-fold, metaphase plates ~3-fold, and spindles ~2-fold over early cleavage divisions, with spindle volume continuing to scale even when length plateaus.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C7-C13 are well-supported by whole-embryo immunofluorescence data (Figure 1) showing continuous scaling relationships and quantified fold-changes across developmental stages. The measurements use appropriate 3D confocal microscopy and segmentation methods, with three biological replicates providing robust statistical support.

results.result: Individual mitotic chromosomes decrease in length approximately 2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8, with minimal width changes (~1.2-fold increase), indicating that length-wise compaction is the primary mechanism of chromosome scaling. Stage 3 endogenous chromosomes are statistically indistinguishable from replicated sperm chromosomes in egg extracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 are supported by direct measurements of single chromosomes from embryo extracts (Figure 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The use of replicated sperm chromosomes as a proxy for early embryonic chromosomes (C17-C18) is validated by statistical comparison, though this equivalence should be interpreted cautiously as it relies on in vitro reconstitution.

results.result: Mitotic chromosome size cannot be reset by cytoplasmic factors during metaphase, unlike spindles and nuclei. Mixing egg and stage 8 extracts, or adding sperm nuclei to stage 8 metaphase extracts, fails to alter chromosome size, indicating that chromosome scaling factors are set during interphase and are not exchangeable during metaphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19-C24 are well-supported by extract mixing experiments (Figure 2B, 2D) showing no chromosome size changes when cytoplasmic factors are exchanged during metaphase. The conclusion that this mechanism is fundamentally distinct from spindle/nuclear scaling is justified by comparison to published work showing cytoplasmic factor exchange can reset those structures.

results.result: G2-arrested embryo nuclei added to egg extracts produce chromosomes ~2-fold shorter than replicated sperm chromosomes, demonstrating that chromosome size is determined prior to metaphase entry. This size difference persists in clarified extracts lacking spindles, though the magnitude is reduced (1.4-fold vs 2-fold), suggesting spindle/membrane factors may contribute partially.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by experiments using G2-arrested nuclei (Figure 3A-B) and clarified extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). However, the interpretation that spindle/membrane factors 'may contribute' (C30) is speculative and marked as such in the evidence. The reduced effect in clarified extracts could have alternative explanations not fully explored.

results.result: Mitotic chromosome size does not correlate with nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density, or spindle size. Embryo nuclei are 2-fold larger than sperm nuclei (consistent with diploid vs haploid DNA content), yet produce 2-fold shorter chromosomes in egg extracts, while spindles formed with either nucleus type are indistinguishable in size.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are supported by measurements of nuclear diameters, chromosome lengths, and spindle sizes (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The inference that these structures scale independently (C35-C36) is well-justified by the data, though it contradicts the in vivo correlation observed in C2, highlighting the importance of distinguishing in vitro from in vivo mechanisms.

results.result: While chromosome size scaling is recapitulated when embryo nuclei are added to egg extracts, chromosome morphology differs—X-shaped chromosomes with separated sister chromatid arms seen in embryo extracts are not observed in egg extracts. This indicates that size-determining factors remain chromatin-associated while morphology-determining factors do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by visual comparison of chromosome morphologies (Figure 2A vs 3C). The inference that different factors control size versus morphology (C39-C40) is reasonable but somewhat speculative, as the molecular identities of these factors are not determined. Alternative explanations for morphological differences are not fully explored.

results.result: Short embryo chromosomes contain less condensin I and topo II but more histone H1.8 compared to long sperm chromosomes. Condensin II is also lower on embryo chromosomes. These differential protein abundances may contribute to chromosome scaling, consistent with published functional studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C44, C47 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3-4). Claims C42-C43, C45-C46 citing published work are appropriately referenced. The conclusion that these factors 'may contribute' (C47) is appropriately cautious, as correlation does not prove causation without functional perturbation experiments.

results.result: Short embryo chromosomes can be lengthened by cycling through an additional interphase in egg extracts, with condensin I levels increasing 2-fold (the largest change among tested factors) and returning to sperm chromosome levels. This suggests condensin I can override H1.8 compaction activity to lengthen chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by anaphase cycling experiments with immunofluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The inference that condensin I can override H1.8 (C51-C52) is reasonable given that condensin I increased more than H1.8 while chromosomes lengthened, though direct functional tests would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Hi-C analysis reveals that short embryo chromosomes have increased longer-range genomic contacts, larger DNA loops (10^5-10^6 bp vs 10^4-10^5 bp), and more DNA per layer (10^7 bp vs 10^6 bp) compared to sperm chromosomes. Combined with condensin I data, this supports a model where decreased condensin I recruitment results in larger loops and length-wise compaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are supported by Hi-C data (Figure 4A-C) showing clear differences in contact probability curves and their derivatives. The interpretation of loop and layer sizes (C56-C57) relies on published models, which is appropriate. The integrated model (C58) combining Hi-C and immunofluorescence data is well-reasoned, though only two biological replicates were performed for Hi-C.

results.result: Increasing nuclear-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio in vitro by varying sperm nuclei concentration decreases chromosome length ~1.3-fold with ~1.6-fold decreased condensin I, consistent with in vivo metaphase plate scaling. However, N/C ratio does not affect nuclear size and actually increases spindle size, indicating it specifically scales chromosomes but not other structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C59-C64 are supported by experiments varying nuclei concentration (Figure 5B-E). The conclusion that N/C ratio specifically scales chromosomes (C64) is well-justified by the differential effects on different structures. However, the unexpected spindle size increase (C63) is not mechanistically explained and warrants further investigation.

results.result: While previous studies showed nuclei and spindles scale to compartment volume through limiting-component mechanisms, maternal components do not become size-limiting for these structures at the N/C ratios tested here (~10-fold lower than in encapsulation studies), suggesting limiting-component mechanisms operate only at later developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 appropriately cite published work (C65) and make a reasonable inference (C66) based on comparing N/C ratio ranges between studies. The conclusion is consistent with the observation that nuclear size did not decrease and spindle size increased with higher N/C ratio, contrary to limiting-component predictions.

results.result: The factors that set chromosome length as a function of N/C ratio are loaded during interphase, not metaphase. Varying stage 8 embryo nuclei concentration in metaphase extracts has no effect, and adding unreplicated sperm chromosomes directly to metaphase extracts also shows no N/C ratio effect, indicating titration occurs during interphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by control experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-B) showing that N/C ratio only affects chromosome size when nuclei undergo interphase in the extract. The logic is sound and the experiments appropriately control for the timing of factor loading.

results.result: Protein concentrations in embryos remain constant during early cleavage divisions, but levels of condensin I, H3, and H1.8 in interphase nuclei decrease as genome copy number increases. This confirms that maternal factors are titratable and demonstrates that increased N/C ratio is sufficient to shorten chromosomes, likely by decreasing condensin I levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by Western blots (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) and immunofluorescence of nuclei from different stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B). The data directly demonstrate the titration effect in vivo, validating the in vitro N/C ratio experiments. The mechanistic link to condensin I (C75) is well-supported by the combined data.

results.result: Importin α partitioning scales mitotic chromosomes to cell surface area/volume ratio during metaphase. Palmostatin treatment (mimicking higher SA/V) decreases chromosome size, which is rescued by non-palmitoylatable importin α but not wild-type. This occurs through increased H1.8 availability without changing condensin I or topo II levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C76-C82 are supported by palmostatin experiments with rescue by non-palmitoylatable importin α (Figure 6B-D). The specificity of the rescue (C80) provides strong evidence for the mechanism. However, the model that importin α directly regulates H1.8 availability (C82) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated—H1.8 could be an indirect target.

results.result: Palmostatin treatment during metaphase is sufficient to shrink chromosomes, while treatment during interphase has no effect. This demonstrates that importin α partitioning scales chromosomes specifically during metaphase in a condensin I-independent pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by cell cycle stage-specific palmostatin treatment experiments (Figure 6F). The temporal specificity (metaphase vs interphase) is clearly demonstrated. The conclusion that this is condensin I-independent (C85) is justified by the immunofluorescence data showing unchanged condensin I levels with palmostatin treatment.

results.result: Mitotic chromosome scaling involves two temporally distinct pathways: N/C ratio during interphase (acting through condensin I) and importin α partitioning during metaphase (acting through H1.8). Both interphase and metaphase phases contribute to chromosome scaling, with condensin I acting only in the N/C ratio pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87, C91-C92 synthesize findings from multiple experiments. The temporal separation is well-demonstrated by the cell cycle stage-specific effects. The pathway-specific roles of condensin I (N/C ratio) versus H1.8 (importin α) are supported by comparing immunofluorescence data (Figure 5C vs 6D). This represents a well-integrated model of the overall findings.

results.result: Although spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes scale coordinately in vivo, the mechanisms regulating their size changes are distinct. In egg extracts, chromosome size does not correlate with spindle or nuclear size, and varying N/C ratio affects these structures differently (chromosomes shrink 1.3-fold, spindles increase 2-fold, nuclei unchanged).
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by comparing in vivo observations (Figure 1) with in vitro experiments (Figures 3, 5). The conclusion that mechanisms are distinct despite coordinate scaling in vivo is well-justified. This represents an important conceptual advance, distinguishing correlation from mechanistic coupling.

results.result: The authors speculate that N/C ratio during interphase sets chromosome size within a range, while importin α partitioning during metaphase sets final size to ensure metaphase plate scales with spindle size, potentially preventing chromosome mis-segregation as proposed in earlier models.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are explicitly speculative (C94 marked as speculation in evidence). While the model is consistent with the data showing two pathways, direct evidence for hierarchical regulation or coordination with spindle size to prevent mis-segregation is lacking. Claim C95 cites a published model but does not test it experimentally. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future work rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Within physiologically relevant condensin I concentrations, less condensin I correlates with increased loop size and length-wise compaction. Condensin I can act independently of H1.8 to lengthen chromosomes and is the major scaling factor, though H1.8 can also modulate size independently, indicating condensin I is not the only factor determining chromosome size in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 integrate data from multiple experiments (anaphase cycling, N/C ratio, importin α) with published work. The conclusion that condensin I is the major but not sole scaling factor (C100, C103) is well-supported. The nuanced interpretation acknowledging complexity in vivo (C101) is appropriate. However, some conclusions rely on comparing this study to published work with different experimental designs (C98-C99).

results.result: The authors propose that N/C ratio could be a universal mechanism for regulating chromatin structure across the cell cycle, affecting transcriptional regulation (ZGA) during interphase and chromosome segregation during metaphase. Recent studies suggest increasing nuclear import rates trigger ZGA by providing access to pioneer factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 appropriately cites published work on ZGA. However, claims C105-C106 are largely speculative, extrapolating from the current findings to broader principles. While the hypothesis is interesting and consistent with published work, the current study does not directly test transcriptional regulation or ZGA. The connection between N/C ratio effects on chromosome size versus transcription is inferred rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Background claims establishing that mitotic chromosomes scale with cell size across metazoans, that chromosome size affects segregation fidelity, that various mechanisms regulate subcellular scaling, and that Xenopus provides a powerful system for studying these phenomena through both in vivo and in vitro approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C107-C119 are appropriately cited from published literature and represent established knowledge motivating the study. Claim C120 summarizes the main findings. These background claims are well-supported by citations and provide appropriate context, though they are not novel results of this study.
